title: Making Flexible Work Real for Disabled People: employers, law and culture
label: 21 October 2026 · Flexible working & disability
summary: Witnesses from the Trades Union Congress and Business Disability Forum told the Committee that many employers have reached practical limits on flexibility without reorganising, disabled workers routinely face long waits and partial or missing reasonable adjustments, and that law, guidance and enforcement need strengthening. They called for clearer practical guidance, faster and better-funded support (including changes to Access to Work), stronger legal rights such as advertising flexibility and a default right to flexible working, independent verification of employer schemes, and careful use of return-to-office mandates.

chapters.title: Employers' practical limits and where problems arise
chapters.takeaway: Large employers say they've offered much flexibility already but reach organisational limits, especially where roles must be frontline or location-based.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Angela, you said some businesses report they've reached the limit of what flexibility they can offer. Which businesses tell you that?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: We work mainly with very large employers—tens to hundreds of thousands of staff. They tell us they've already redeployed people, given adjustments, and introduced flexible working, but that can change the shape of the organisation.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Problems show up most in firms with a mix of desk-based and front-facing roles—NHS, police, retail—where you can't make every role remote or part-time without reorganising.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Could employers do more to organise roles so they're more inclusive?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: They could, but retraining and upskilling take time and money—especially in smaller organisations. Employers often look for existing vacancies that match someone's skills rather than invest in training.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Unions told us employers sometimes don't consult or think creatively. We've seen part-time requests refused without exploring job sharing, and employers failing to give evidence for refusals.

chapters.title: Guidance, audits and examples of what works
chapters.takeaway: Clear, practical guidance and sector-specific case studies help employers find workable flexible solutions; role audits can show where flexibility is possible.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Is clearer guidance across sectors likely to increase employer uptake?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Yes—big employers have very different roles. Some jobs can be output-focused and highly flexible; others cannot. Employers should audit roles to decide what's full-time-only and what's adaptable.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: We need both guidance and stronger rules. Our reps see good collective agreements where unions are strong, but in less unionised sectors stronger law helps. Employers also need practical examples of how to make services work.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: We run fora where employers swap stories. Line managers often support flexibility but getting structural sign-off up the chain causes delays and frustrates employees.

chapters.title: Legal fixes and enforcement: what witnesses want changed
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want faster, clearer processes, legal changes to encourage flexible working and advertising of options, and stronger enforcement and funding for the EHRC.

turns.speaker: Nadia Whittome
turns.text: TUC, most disabled workers who request reasonable adjustments don't get them fully—why is that?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Barriers are multiple: many fear rejection so don't ask; among those who do, over half got only some or none of needed adjustments. Employers give vague refusals, cite impracticality or cost, or even say someone isn't 'disabled enough.'

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Access to Work is underused and slow: spending rose but it reaches only about 1% of working disabled people, and the NAO found employers failed to make adjustments in many cases.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: We need the EHRC better funded. Its staff and budget are far smaller than in 2007, so it can't enforce rights or pursue targeted employer action effectively.

turns.speaker: Nadia Whittome
turns.text: Would updated guidance alone fix this, or do we need changes to law?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: We need legal changes. The TUC supports making flexible working more of a right—default flexible working, stronger advertising duties, and better tribunal remedies—because voluntary approaches don't always work.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Employers want the ERA to allow them to consider whether a flexible arrangement is sustainable over time. The Equality Act focuses on the 'now'; employers ask to factor in strategic plans when deciding reasonableness.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: We support speeding things up but the cause of delay matters. Decisions can be quick; procurement of adjustments and Access to Work delays take longer, so a two-week deadline needs pragmatic exceptions.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: One practical fix: give Access to Work in-principle awards so employers can accept adjustments while the detailed funding process proceeds.

chapters.title: Advertising flexibility and default flexible working
chapters.takeaway: Publishing flexible options in job adverts and treating flexibility as the norm would broaden applicant pools and help disabled people apply and stay in work.

turns.speaker: Kevin McKenna
turns.text: TUC wants a legal duty to advertise flexible options. Have employers accepted that voluntarily?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Many HR managers say it's easy to include flexible options: our polling showed about 59% of HR managers would find it easy or already do it, and uptake is higher where unions operate.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Advertising flexibility attracts more applicants. Timewise and other studies show only about 30% of jobs currently include this; Zurich advertising flexibility saw a 66% rise in applications and more part-time hires.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: I agree it's sensible but emphasise job description detail. Employers with thousands of roles face a practical challenge to do a flexibility analysis for every role before advertising.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: The TUC proposes roles be deemed suitable for flexible working unless an employer can objectively justify otherwise—mirroring Equality Act tests.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: The devil's in the detail: yes to job-level clarity and good job descriptions, but let's be pragmatic about how much upfront work employers can do across huge role sets.

chapters.title: Return-to-office mandates, supported work and inclusion
chapters.takeaway: Blanket back-to-office rules often lack evidence, harm disabled workers' productivity and wellbeing, and employers need clearer routes into supported internships and progression paths.

turns.speaker: Richard Quigley
turns.text: What's the evidence behind mandates to bring people back to the office?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Research shows mandates often come from senior leaders, not line managers, and they rarely provide solid evidence that more office time boosts collaboration or productivity. Disabled workers often prefer remote or hybrid work.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Work Foundation found 65% of disabled workers wanted to continue remote working. Studies show mandates worsen outcomes for many disabled staff—productivity, work-life balance and health.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Mandates can be well-intentioned—leaders want people together—but they risk excluding disabled people if employers default to keeping them at home or don't invest in getting them into the workplace.

turns.speaker: Richard Quigley
turns.text: Should the Government test mandates?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: If flexible rights in the ERA and reasonable adjustments in the Equality Act work properly, mandates shouldn't be necessary. Good equality impact assessments are important.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Yes—conduct rigorous equality impact assessments, involve unions and equality reps, and avoid blanket rules that disadvantage disabled workers.

turns.speaker: Alex Brewer
turns.text: Only 6% of people with a learning disability are in paid work. What would make a real difference?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Employers need less jargon and clearer routes in. Many are scared of reputational risk. Simple actions—accessible adverts, supportive recruitment partners, and small-scale supported internships—help, but employers need to hear clear examples.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Also, many disabled people are in insecure work and some groupings—like atypical workers—lack rights. Extending flexible-working rights to more categories of worker would help bring people in.

turns.speaker: Alex Brewer
turns.text: And progression?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Think beyond upward promotion. Sideways moves, portfolio careers and adjusted responsibilities all let people progress while managing health or fluctuating conditions.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: But disabled workers worry hybrid working harms promotion prospects. Good line manager practice, inclusive development and union involvement matter for fair progression.

turns.speaker: Alex Brewer
turns.text: What about Disability Confident—does it work?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Unions and disabled workers criticize it as a marketing tool: self-certification, weak standards and no independent checks. We want a replacement co-designed with disabled people, independently verified and with real workforce thresholds.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Employers want a clear three-tier approach: basic compliance, good inclusive practice, and exemplary proactive employers. The scheme could help if it makes compliance clear and practical.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both—this has been very informative. Please send any follow-up material.
